facts.fact_text: On 24 April 2013 the two applicant associations informed the Ministry of the Interior of their intention to hold a peaceful public rally on 17 May 2013 in the centre of Tbilisi to mark the International Day Against Homophobia.

On 1 May 2013 the two applicant associations informed the Ministry of the Interior of their intention to hold a peaceful public rally on 17 May 2013 in the centre of Tbilisi to mark the International Day Against Homophobia.
The planned event (the IDAHO event) would take the form of a silent twenty-minute flash mob.
On 17 May 2013, at around 12 noon, participants in the IDAHO event started gathering at Pushkin Square.
Applicants nos. 15, 19, 21-23, 25, 29, 31-33, 35 and 37 (the group of twelve individual applicants) were the first to arrive at Pushkin Square at 12 noon on 17 May 2013.

At around 12.30 p.m. on 17 May 2013, applicants nos. 2-14, 16 and 36 (the group of fifteen individual applicants) were trying to reach the site of the IDAHO event at Pushkin Square via the narrow Vachnadze Street.
The two cases concern the respondent State's alleged failure to protect the applicants' public rally from homophobic and/or transphobic acts of violence by counter-demonstrators.

On 24 April 2013 the two applicant associations informed the Ministry of the Interior of their intention to hold a peaceful public rally on 17 May 2013 in the centre of Tbilisi to mark the International Day Against Homophobia.

In view of the violence committed by radical groups during a similar event held the previous year (as documented in Identoba and Others v. Georgia, no. 73235/12, §§ 10-19, 12 May 2015), the applicant associations asked the Ministry of the Interior to invest more time and energy in devising an efficient plan to protect the public rally from possible violence.
On 9 May 2013 the applicant associations informed the Ministry of the Interior of serious threats posted on the Internet by various identifiable individuals.

A number of interviews with priests were published in various national newspapers in which several clergymen, including Father J., openly and repeatedly stated that the aim of the 'prayer rally' was to prevent the IDAHO event from taking place.

A number of clearly identifiable individual participants in the forthcoming counter-demonstration intensified a hate speech campaign on social media directed at the two applicant associations' staff members.
During the meetings, Ministry of the Interior officials made formal assurances that no efforts would be spared to guarantee the safety of all the participants in the IDAHO event.
The Ministry of the Interior promised to deploy sufficient manpower to create strong police cordons between the two opposing groups at the IDAHO event.

The 2,000 police officers deployed on 17 May 2013 were tasked with creating cordons separating Pushkin Square, where the applicants were to gather, from all the streets leading to the adjacent Rustaveli Avenue, where the 'prayer rally' was to be held.
The LGBT demonstrators at Pushkin Square were separated from the counter-demonstrators only by removable metal fences and a thin cordon of unarmed and unequipped police patrol officers.
Video footage filmed by independent journalists shows the same clergymen leading the crowd to break through the police cordon with no resistance from the police.

A video-recording filmed by journalists shows a number of police officers disassembling cordons and removing metal fences that had been installed to protect the LGBT demonstrators from the counter-demonstrators.

Video footage contains scenes of police patrol officers discussing an order from the deputy head of the State Security Agency — a structural unit of the Ministry of the Interior under Deputy Minister G.Z.'s direct supervision at the material time — to remove metal fences separating Pushkin Square from Rustaveli Avenue.

Video footage shows certain police patrol officers, who were supposed to block the counter-demonstrators by standing in cordons, opening up gaps for the counter-demonstrators and saying things such as 'go!' and 'pass one by one!' as they passed through.

A video-recording shows a journalist standing in an area adjacent to Pushkin Square asking police patrol officers whether the counter-demonstrators had run over the cordon or whether it had been opened by the police, to which one of the officers replied 'it has been opened.'

Video footage shows that eventually hundreds of counter-demonstrators, led by clergymen, got through the police cordons and headed towards the group of twelve individual applicants and other participants in the IDAHO event gathered at Pushkin Square.

Faced with the approaching mob, the group of twelve individual applicants at Pushkin Square retreated by boarding two buses that had apparently been provided by the police in advance for dispersal purposes.

Frenzied counter-demonstrators surrounded and blocked the buses containing the group of twelve individual applicants and other LGBT demonstrators, rocking the vehicles and throwing stones, wooden sticks and footstools at the windscreens.
The group of fifteen individual applicants (applicants nos. 2-14, 16 and 36) were suddenly encircled by a large number of participants in the 'prayer rally' on Vachnadze Street.

Once the trapped activists boarded the police minibus, the counter-demonstrators, yelling 'stone them all!' and 'kill them all!', surrounded it and broke almost all the windows and the front windscreen with iron batons and stones in an attempt to pull the passengers out.

On 17 May 2013 the Ministry of the Interior launched of its own motion a general inquiry into the acts of violence committed during the clash between the participants in the IDAHO event and those in the 'prayer rally'.
No response was given by the Ministry of the Interior to the complainants' requests of 25 July and 20 September 2013.

On 27 December 2013 the Chief Public Prosecutor's Office responded that there were no signs of illegality in the actions of the police, who had duly discharged their duties during the demonstration by preventing grave consequences which could otherwise have occurred given the disproportionately high number of counter-demonstrators.

The Tbilisi City Court stated that the investigation had failed to secure any evidence that would reliably prove the link between the violent dispersal of the IDAHO event and the actions of the accused on 17 May 2013.

The Tbilisi City Court identified a shortcoming in the investigation consisting of the investigators' failure to properly examine the relevant pieces of video footage of the dispersal, which the court considered crucial evidence that could have allowed for the proper identification of at least some of the perpetrators of the violent attacks.

The Tbilisi City Court identified a further shortcoming in the investigation consisting of the failure to commission a forensic examination of the buses that had been damaged by the mob during the dispersal process.
